fields.apa_citation: Renz, T., Leistner, P., & Liebl, A. (2018). Effects of the location of sound masking loudspeakers on cognitive performance in open-plan offices: Local sound masking is as efficient as conventional sound masking. Applied Acoustics. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apacoust.2018.06.024 [Volume/page numbers not printed in the retrieved text; DOI/journal ID inferred from reference-hub prefix S0003-682X(18) shown in the paper's own reference list formatting.]
fields.main_conclusion: A local, decentralised sound-masking loudspeaker placed near the distracting speech source performed about as well as a conventional ceiling-mounted masking system for improving working-memory performance and reducing annoyance from background speech, and extending the masking spectrum down to 100 Hz (instead of 200 Hz) gave a further, modest performance benefit.
independent_variables: Sound masking emitter location/configuration (local emitter in acoustic screen or cabinet vs. six-emitter conventional ceiling array)
Spatial separation between masker and target speech direction (same direction vs. 90 degrees apart)
Masking spectrum high-pass filter cutoff frequency (100 Hz vs 200 Hz)
dependent_variables: Mean error rate on a serial (number) recall task
fields.construct_pair: Sound-masking emitter location and configuration -> Working-memory (serial recall) performance and perceived annoyance
fields.stimulus_description: Employees performed a serial digit recall task in a modified open-plan office while background speech (recorded German sentences from the Hochmair-Schulz-Moser test) was played from studio monitors simulating two coworkers, combined with pink-noise-based masking sound delivered from either local loudspeakers near the speech sources or a six-emitter ceiling array, at varying SNRs and filter cutoffs, across twelve sound conditions.
fields.methods_surface_summary: One-way repeated-measures laboratory design with 24 employees (25 recruited, one excluded) each tested under all twelve sound conditions (Latin-square counterbalanced) in a controlled open-plan office; performance was scored as percentage of digits recalled incorrectly on a serial recall task, and annoyance was rated after each condition; analyzed with repeated-measures ANOVA and Benjamini-Hochberg-corrected one-tailed paired t-tests against silence and unmasked-speech controls.
measurement_inventory: Speech Transmission Index (STI) / sound pressure level instrumentation (NTi XL2 sound level meter)

notes.apa_citation: Exact volume/page/DOI not visible in the docling text; year (2018) and journal (Applied Acoustics) are stated in the running header; DOI is a plausible reconstruction based on the article's PII prefix appearing in its own reference-hub links, not directly printed.
notes.direction: Rated mixed because the effect of emitter location/spatial separation on performance and annoyance was inconsistent across SNR levels and control comparisons -- e.g., local masking helped at -9 dB SNR when co-located with speech but the 90-degree-separated condition sometimes performed worse than silence, and some paired comparisons (e.g., conventional vs. local at -9 dB) showed no significant difference.
notes.sample_n: 25 employees were recruited but one subject's data were excluded due to equipment failure, leaving 24 for the serial-recall performance analysis (Fig. 3, n=24); the annoyance analysis further dropped to n=21 because three subjects' questionnaire data did not load.
notes.p_value: This is the omnibus repeated-measures ANOVA main effect of sound condition on serial-recall mean error rate, F(11,253)=3.48, p<0.001 -- the paper's headline statistical result for cognitive performance; effects for individual paired comparisons vary (see Table 3).
notes.effect_size: Reported as the omnibus eta-squared for the performance ANOVA (eta^2=0.13); the parallel omnibus effect for annoyance was much larger (eta^2=0.63), and individual paired-comparison Cohen's d values ranged from about 0.18 to 5.1 across different contrasts (see Tables 3-4).
